title: When to bypass the ORM
description: Learn the specific scenarios where dropping down to raw SQL, stored procedures, or Dapper produces measurably better results than staying inside EF Core's abstraction.

data.text: EF Core is the right default for most .NET data access, but it is not always the fastest path to the database. Knowing when to bypass the ORM — and how to do so cleanly — separates competent developers from senior engineers who optimize at the right layer.
Signs that the ORM is the bottleneck

items: LINQ translation generates a query plan that is measurably slower than hand-written SQL.
Bulk inserts or updates touch thousands of rows and `SaveChanges()` is the bottleneck.
A reporting or analytics query requires CTEs, window functions, or database hints that LINQ cannot express cleanly.
Query profiling shows the translation phase itself consuming meaningful CPU time on hot paths.
Third-party database features like JSON operators, full-text search, or geospatial queries are not fully supported through EF Core mappings.

data.title: Measure before optimizing
data.text: Profile with real production data volumes and realistic concurrency before bypassing the ORM. LINQ translation overhead is rarely the dominant cost. I/O waits, network latency, and missing indexes usually matter more.

EF Core's `SaveChanges()` is optimized for individual or small-batch writes. For bulk inserts, updates, or deletes, each entity goes through change detection and generates separate SQL statements. EFCore.BulkExtensions or raw `SqlBulkCopy` can insert tens of thousands of rows in a fraction of the time.

data.title: Bulk insert with EFCore.BulkExtensions

data.text: Reporting endpoints often need complex aggregations, grouping, and ranking that are easier to express in SQL than in LINQ. Using `FromSqlRaw` or Dapper lets you write the exact query the database should run, with full access to CTEs, window functions, and database hints.

data.title: Reporting query with FromSqlRaw
data.code:
var monthlyRevenue = await dbContext.MonthlyRevenueReports
    .FromSqlRaw(@"
        WITH MonthlySales AS (
            SELECT YEAR(OrderDate) AS Year,
                   MONTH(OrderDate) AS Month,
                   SUM(TotalAmount) AS Revenue
            FROM Orders
            WHERE OrderDate >= @StartDate
            GROUP BY YEAR(OrderDate), MONTH(OrderDate)
        )
        SELECT Year, Month, Revenue,
               LAG(Revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY Year ORDER BY Month) AS PrevMonthRevenue
        FROM MonthlySales",
        new { StartDate = DateTime.UtcNow.AddYears(-1) })
    .ToListAsync();

data.text: Some teams maintain stored procedures for mission-critical or heavily optimized operations. EF Core can call stored procedures via `FromSqlRaw` for queries or `ExecuteSqlRaw` for commands. The stored procedure handles the logic inside the database, and EF Core handles the result mapping.

data.title: Calling a stored procedure with FromSqlRaw
data.code:
var topProducts = await dbContext.TopSellingProducts
    .FromSqlRaw("EXEC GetTopSellingProducts @CategoryId, @TopCount",
        new SqlParameter("@CategoryId", categoryId),
        new SqlParameter("@TopCount", 10))
    .ToListAsync();

data.text: When you bypass EF Core, keep the raw SQL isolated in a repository or query class rather than scattering it across controllers and services. This makes it easy to audit, test, and replace. Document why each bypass exists so future maintainers understand the performance justification.

items: Profile the current EF Core query and confirm the bottleneck before bypassing.
Isolate raw SQL in dedicated repository methods or query types.
Map raw SQL results to read-only DTOs rather than tracked entities.
Document the performance justification for each bypass.
Revisit bypassed queries periodically — newer EF Core versions may support them natively.

data.title: Key takeaways
items: Bypass the ORM for bulk writes, complex reporting, and database-specific features.
Measure first — I/O and indexing are usually bigger wins than translation speed.
Isolate raw SQL in repositories and map to DTOs, not tracked entities.
Document every bypass so the codebase stays maintainable.
